title: The performance arts: reviews and critiques
subtitle: gripping, panned, a standing ovation
summary: Review a play, film or concert like a critic - from hackneyed plots and harrowing documentaries to glowing reviews, standing ovations and total flops.

lesson.heading: Negative adjectives for a work or performance
lesson.text: Something **overrated** is not as good as people say. A plot that is **hackneyed** has been done so often it is boring. A play that is **disjointed** is unconnected and not in a clear order, and a story that is **far-fetched** is impossible to believe. Something long and boring is **tedious**.

examples.text: The play was **disjointed** and difficult to follow.
The film Green Aliens from Mars was a bit **far-fetched**.

lesson.heading: Positive (and shocking) adjectives
lesson.text: A **gripping** film is exciting and keeps your attention the whole time. A **harrowing** documentary is extremely upsetting; a **moving** story makes you feel pity or sadness. A performance you remember long afterwards is **memorable** or **unforgettable**; one done in a simple but attractive style is **understated**. A comedian who is extremely funny is **hilarious**. A play that goes against accepted social standards and is likely to shock is **risque**.

examples.text: It was a **gripping** film from start to finish.
It was a **harrowing** documentary about war and refugee camps.
It's a **moving** story about a child whose mother dies.
The play was a bit **risque**, and some religious leaders criticised it.
examples.note: risque usually takes a modifier: rather, very, a bit

lesson.note: All these adjectives work for writing too: the plot of the novel is far-fetched / gripping / hilarious.

left.label: A hit
left.text: The **applause** was **deafening**, so the show got **glowing reviews** - excellent ones. Critics may call the work a **masterpiece**, a very great work of art.
examples: The audience called for several **encores** after his concert.
She got a **standing ovation** as Juliet in Romeo and Juliet.
Her latest album has already won three **awards**.
Sam Dell won the award for 'Best **up-and-coming** actor'.

right.label: A failure
right.text: A work that is **panned** or **slated** is very negatively criticised - the opposite of being **universally lauded**, highly praised by everyone.
examples: His latest opera was **panned** by the critics.
The play **bombed** in London's West End.
The show was **booed** on the first night.
The new TV soap has turned out to be a total **flop**.

lesson.heading: Casting
lesson.text: An actor who is **miscast** is the wrong person for the role and comes across as **unconvincing** - not seeming real or true. An actor always associated with one type of role has been **typecast**.

examples.text: Novak was definitely **miscast** as the father in that film; he was very **unconvincing**.
She has become **typecast** as a middle-aged mother in TV drama series.

lesson.heading: Nouns relating to performing
rows: a short performance where actors show what they can do, hoping to get a role
practice performances before the real thing
the way a performer understands and performs a song or role
one of several performances of a work that exist
a version of a song that is not the original
the picture an actor creates of a person

lesson.heading: The language of film reviews
lesson.text: Reviewers reach for the same handful of words. A **blockbuster** is a film huge numbers of people will go and see; a **cliffhanger** keeps you in suspense; a film that **keeps you on the edge of your seat** keeps you constantly excited. A **budding** star is one just beginning to develop, like the bud of a flower - much the same idea as up-and-coming. A **cops-and-robbers** film has a police or crime theme.

examples.text: In this latest **blockbuster** cops-and-robbers movie, **budding** Hollywood star Fletch Packline plays a country boy who gets involved with a gang of criminals.
Packline's **portrayal** of the confused small-town boy is convincing, but Julia Fischer is somewhat **miscast**.
Not a **masterpiece**, but it will certainly **keep you on the edge of your seat**.

lesson.text: Panned, slated and bombed are all about failure; lauded and glowing are about praise - and only people boo, only critics pan.

exercises.prompt: Match each word with the adjective that is opposite in meaning.
I can't remember the last time I saw such a ___ film - it held my attention from start to finish.
exercises.explanation: A gripping film is exciting and keeps your attention the whole time.

exercises.prompt: Her dance performance was ___, simply marvellous - I still think about it years later.
exercises.explanation: A memorable or unforgettable performance stays with you long after you have seen it.

exercises.prompt: It's a ___ film - it's difficult to watch without getting very upset.
exercises.explanation: A harrowing film or documentary is extremely upsetting.

exercises.prompt: His first stand-up routine had the audience falling off their seats - it was absolutely ___.
The musical was rather ___ and was attacked by several politicians and religious figures.
exercises.explanation: Risque means against accepted social standards and likely to shock some people; it usually takes a modifier such as rather or a bit.

exercises.prompt: The musical Dogs turned out to be a total ___ and closed after ten days.
exercises.explanation: A flop is a complete failure; you can also say the show bombed.

exercises.prompt: It was loudly ___ by the audience on the first night.
exercises.explanation: To boo is to make disapproving noises at a performance.

exercises.prompt: The show was ___ by the critics, who had praise only for the male lead.
exercises.explanation: To pan or slate a work is to criticise it very negatively.

exercises.prompt: Danger, however, has received ___ reviews and has been given a standing ovation at every performance.
What do we call the picture an actor creates of a character?
exercises.explanation: A portrayal is the picture an actor creates of a person; an audition is the short performance that wins them the role.

exercises.prompt: Which word describes a young actor who is likely to become very successful?
exercises.explanation: A budding star is just beginning to develop, like the bud of a flower; up-and-coming means the same.

exercises.statement: A cover is the original recording of a song.
exercises.explanation: Wrong - a cover is a version of a song that is not the original. I prefer the original version by the Beatles.

exercises.statement: If an actor is typecast, they are always associated with the same type of role.
exercises.explanation: Correct - she has become typecast as a middle-aged mother in TV drama series.

exercises.prompt: Would you find each word in a good review or a bad one?
Put this line from a film review in order.
exercises.answer: Not a masterpiece, but it will keep you on the edge of your seat
exercises.explanation: To keep someone on the edge of their seat is to keep them constantly excited and in suspense.
